hints: Walk around nums as if it were a circle (the last element is followed by the first). In a rotated sorted array, how many times can the values go down?
Count the 'drops' where nums[i] > nums[(i+1) % n], wrapping around at the end. A sorted-then-rotated array has at most one drop.

1. drops = 0.
  2. For i from 0 to n−1: if nums[i] > nums[(i + 1) % n], drops++.
  3. Return drops <= 1.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try all n rotations and check whether any of them is non-decreasing.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Count descents around the circle; a rotated sorted array has at most one.

explain: For nums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], comparing neighbours in a circle gives 3≤4, 4≤5, 5>1 (one drop), 1≤2, and the wrap-around 2≤3, so there is exactly one drop and the function returns true. The single drop is the 'cut' where the rotation happened; a second drop means no rotation can fix it, as in [2, 1, 3, 4] (drops at 2>1 and at the wrap-around 4>2). An array of all equal values has zero drops and is also true.
recognize: "Could this be a sorted array that was rotated" → count descents around the circle; at most one is allowed.
